Demystifying On-Policy Distillation:
Where Does the Teacher’s Advantage Live?

Yiping Li    Zhibo Hou    Fan Zhao    Zhiyu An    Wan Du Affiliation: University of California, Merced, USA Email: {yipingli,zhou6,fanzhao,zan7,wdu3}@ucmerced.edu
Abstract

On-policy distillation (OPD) is increasingly studied as a cheaper alternative to reinforcement learning, yet it remains a form of knowledge distillation (KD) that relies on teacher supervision. We revisit OPD from the KD perspective by asking where the teacher’s advantage lies along student-generated trajectories. Controlled token flips at teacher–student disagreements directly measure the accuracy gained from teacher corrections. Single-token flips yield a modest average gain on selected failed trajectories, whereas repeated flips raise accuracy from 28.4% to 74.5%, close to the teacher’s 76.9%. Gains continue to accumulate with more flips, but mass- and KL-based selection outperform random flips by 15–18 percentage points at counts of similar magnitude. Selective intervention remains useful after OPD, but greater argmax agreement does not consistently improve accuracy across model pairs. We advocate training schedules that learn more valuable teacher corrections while maintaining distributional stability. Controlled flips and fork-resolution analysis evaluate OPD beyond accuracy by measuring which teacher preferences the student acquires and what further correction can recover.

1 Introduction

Reinforcement learning improves large language models after pretraining, but it is expensive (DeepSeek-AI, 2025; Yang et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025). On-policy distillation (OPD) offers a cheaper route by training the student on its own rollouts toward a teacher’s next-token distribution (Agarwal et al., 2024; Lu and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025). Reported results reach RL-level accuracy at about a tenth of the cost (Yang et al., 2025; Lu and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025). This efficiency has brought OPD into frontier post-training pipelines and attracted research interest (DeepSeek-AI, 2026; Xiaomi LLM-Core Team, 2026; GLM-5-Team, 2026; Kimi Team, 2026; Yang et al., 2026b; Song and Zheng, 2026).

Yet OPD is commonly treated as an RL method because it serves as a cheaper substitute for RL in post-training. This view captures its role in the pipeline, but OPD still depends on a teacher and remains a form of knowledge distillation (KD). In conventional KD, soft labels preserve similarities that hard labels discard (Hinton et al., 2015). For OPD, however, it remains unclear what in the teacher’s next-token distributions contributes to better reasoning and where that contribution appears along the student’s trajectory.

Prior work suggests that distillation quality depends on both what the teacher provides and what the student can learn (Li et al., 2022). Therefore, OPD training outcomes alone do not distinguish the teacher’s available advantage from the student’s ability to acquire it. We first examine the teacher’s contribution through interventions that hold the student’s parameters fixed, then analyze how OPD checkpoints change the disagreement.

In this paper, we focus on forks, positions at which the student and teacher diverge in their next-token preferences. We measure the teacher’s advantage over the student through single and repeated token flips. A single flip replaces the student’s token at one fork and lets the student continue. Dual-track decoding repeats this one-token intervention at selected forks as the trajectory develops.

We use these interventions to ask how much accuracy teacher corrections recover and whether selecting particular forks improves that recovery. Checkpoint analysis then asks which preferences OPD acquires and whether learning them produces better answers. Our contributions are the following.

  • •

    We develop an intervention-based evaluation of OPD. Controlled flips measure the accuracy recoverable through teacher corrections, while checkpoint analysis measures which teacher preferences the student acquires. This separates the value of supervision from its learnability.

  • •

    We characterize how teacher corrections improve student trajectories. Gains accumulate through repeated flips, but mass- and KL-based selection recover more accuracy than random flips at intervention counts of similar magnitude. Teacher guidance is therefore broadly useful without making all disagreements equally valuable.

  • •

    We identify a mismatch between token-level learning and trajectory-level improvement. Across model pairs, fork resolution can increase while accuracy stagnates or declines, and selective intervention remains useful after training. Resolving disagreements alone cannot establish whether OPD turns teacher guidance into better answers.

2 Related Work

On-policy distillation and its variants.

OPD trains on student-generated trajectories with teacher supervision, often using reverse KL (Agarwal et al., 2024; Lu and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025). TA-OPD retains high-teachability tokens, with a 10% budget in its main experiments (Wang et al., 2026c), while TIP emphasizes low-entropy tokens with high teacher–student divergence (Xu et al., 2026b). Prefix methods study shorter rollouts and supervision from early trajectory segments (Zhang et al., 2026a; Zhou et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2026b).

Other methods modify supervision through advantage regulation or baselines (Wang et al., 2026b; Zhao et al., 2026; Oh et al., 2026), support-aware matching, asymmetric objectives, or reward extrapolation (Fu et al., 2026; Jia et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026a). EOPD adds forward KL at high-teacher-entropy positions (Jin et al., 2026), while TrOPD chooses the divergence using a trust region on the teacher-to-student ratio (Xing et al., 2026). TGPO supervises teacher-preferred tokens on student-generated prefixes without intervening in generation (Liu et al., 2026c).

Teacher intervention instead changes the rollout through reflection-triggered handoffs (Xu et al., 2026a), backtracking or prefix refinement (Wang et al., 2026a; Jiang et al., 2026), or trust-region behavior blending during warm-up (Plyusov et al., 2026). Other work changes the data or reference (Liu et al., 2026b; Luo et al., 2026; Hou et al., 2026), and Song and Zheng (2026) survey OPD.

These rules encode different assumptions about where the teacher’s advantage lies. They favor sparse positions, uncertain positions, prefixes, or reflection words, but they do not directly test whether the advantage is localized in any of them. We instead ask where the teacher’s higher trajectory-level accuracy enters the student’s trajectory.

Analyses of OPD.

A smaller line of work studies OPD rather than extending it. Li et al. (2026) examine which teachers help which students by tracking how their distributions move during training. Wang et al. (2026b) study the role and failure modes of OPD through training curves across teachers and benchmarks. Luo et al. (2026) connect instability to the dynamics of the per-token advantage. These analyses take the training run as their object, so the outcome combines what the teacher offers with what the student learns. Our interventions isolate the teacher’s contribution with fixed student parameters, and checkpoint comparisons separately track changes in token-level disagreement.

Assisted and guided decoding.

Combining models during decoding has been used both as a method and as a lens for analysis. Speculative decoding lets a large model accept or replace tokens drafted by a smaller model, with speed as the objective (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023). Contrastive decoding and proxy tuning combine model predictions to improve the generated sequence (Li et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024). We use a lockstep teacher–student pairing as a measurement in which the student retains its sampled token unless the intervention selects the position. The number and location of teacher substitutions then become the quantities of interest.

3 Preliminaries

On-policy distillation.

Let πS\pi_{S} be the student and πT\pi_{T} the teacher. Given a prompt PP, OPD trains on the student’s own trajectories x=(x1,…,xT)∼πS(⋅∣P)x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{T})\sim\pi_{S}(\cdot\mid P) of length TT. At every position tt the two models see the same prefix and propose a next token: qt=πS(⋅∣P,x<t)q_{t}=\pi_{S}(\cdot\mid P,x_{<t}) is the student’s distribution and pt=πT(⋅∣P,x<t)p_{t}=\pi_{T}(\cdot\mid P,x_{<t}) the teacher’s. The objective pays, at every position, a weighted price for being different from the teacher:

ℒ=𝔼x∼πS∑t=1TwtKLt,KLt=KL(qt∥pt).\mathcal{L}=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\pi_{S}}\!\sum_{t=1}^{T}w_{t}\mathrm{KL}_{t},\quad\mathrm{KL}_{t}=\mathrm{KL}(q_{t}\|p_{t}). (1)

where wtw_{t} is the weight of position tt, with wt≡1w_{t}\equiv 1 for uniform supervision. Summing over the whole vocabulary at every position is expensive, so our top-kk approximation keeps the tokens the student ranks highest, with k=16k=16:

KLt≈KL^t=∑x∈Topk​(qt)qt​(x)​log⁡qt​(x)pt​(x).\mathrm{KL}_{t}\approx\widehat{\mathrm{KL}}_{t}=\!\!\sum_{x\in\mathrm{Top}_{k}(q_{t})}\!\!q_{t}(x)\log\frac{q_{t}(x)}{p_{t}(x)}. (2)

The gradient therefore reaches only tokens the student already considers plausible; a teacher token outside Topk​(qt)\mathrm{Top}_{k}(q_{t}) is never pushed up directly.

Choice of divergence.

Equation 1 uses the reverse KL, which is mode-seeking: the student is charged for probability it places where the teacher places little. GKD also considers forward KL and Jensen–Shannon (Agarwal et al., 2024), while TrOPD uses a position-dependent mix of reverse and forward KL (Xing et al., 2026). Our experiments use reverse KL throughout.

4 Setup

4.1 Models, Data, and Grading

The student πS\pi_{S} is Qwen3-1.7B in non-thinking mode; the teacher πT\pi_{T} is Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 (Yang et al., 2025). They share a tokenizer, so tokens compare position by position. Problems come from DAPO-Math-17k (Yu et al., 2025). A trajectory is correct when its final Answer:/\boxed expression is equivalent to the reference. Unless stated otherwise both models sample at temperature 0.70.7, top-pp 0.950.95, and teacher-alone baselines use the same sampling. All runs use a fixed seed of 0; the hardware, software and decoding settings of every stage are listed in App. A.

4.2 Fork Definitions and Scores

Fork.

A fork is a position where the student and teacher prefer different next tokens under the same prefix,

arg⁡max⁡qt≠arg⁡max⁡pt,\arg\max q_{t}\neq\arg\max p_{t}, (3)

while the strength of their disagreement is measured separately below. A sampled student token can still equal the teacher’s argmax at a fork, so a fork need not produce a token replacement.

Token mass.

KL measures distribution-level disagreement but is unbounded and is not a metric (Cover and Thomas, 2006). We also use token mass to distinguish two directions of disagreement: the teacher assigning little probability to the student’s token, and the student assigning little probability to the teacher’s choice. For a token set SS, these probabilities are

μtT​(S)=∑x∈Spt​(x),μtS​(S)=∑x∈Sqt​(x),\mu^{T}_{t}(S)=\sum_{x\in S}p_{t}(x),\qquad\mu^{S}_{t}(S)=\sum_{x\in S}q_{t}(x), (4)

and SS can be a single token or a top-kk set, for example {xt}\{x_{t}\} or Topk​(qt)\mathrm{Top}_{k}(q_{t}). Similar quantities appear in prior work (Xing et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026a; Wang et al., 2026c).

Flip.

A flip replaces the student’s token xtx_{t} at a fork with a teacher token, either sampled from ptp_{t} or chosen as its argmax. Each experiment specifies the replacement rule and continuation model. Changing one token does not make the subsequent continuation a teacher-generated trajectory.

Blind Forks.

A fork is blind when the teacher’s preferred token lies outside the student’s top-kk candidates, arg⁡max⁡pt∉Topk​(qt)\arg\max p_{t}\notin\mathrm{Top}_{k}(q_{t}), with k=16k=16. The teacher’s preferred token therefore has no explicit supervision term in the top-kk loss. A reverse-blind fork instead has the student’s token outside the teacher’s top-kk candidates, xt∉Topk​(pt)x_{t}\notin\mathrm{Top}_{k}(p_{t}).

Reflection words.

We use the 13-word list of Relay-OPD (Xu et al., 2026a), including wait, but, and actually, matched at the token level (Section A.4.1). This operational definition includes words that can also occur outside reflection.

4.3 Interventions

Single flip.

One fork of an existing student trajectory is flipped and nothing else before it is changed. The teacher supplies a sampled segment of LL tokens, including the first replacement, and the student then writes the rest of the trajectory. At L=∞L=\infty the teacher finishes the trajectory. The baseline independently resamples the student from the same prefix, including the fork token, to measure gain over another student continuation.

Dual-track decoding.

We use dual-track decoding as a controlled intervention on student generation. Both models condition on the current prefix, with one forward pass each per step. At each fork selected by the flip condition, we replace only the student’s next token with the teacher’s argmax, arg⁡max⁡pt\arg\max p_{t}, then return control to the student. At all other positions, the student samples from its own distribution. Replacements stop once an answer marker appears. We also test sampling the replacement from the teacher’s distribution while keeping the same selection rule (Table 15). This measures the combined effect of repeated token replacements along the resulting trajectory.

5 Empirical Analysis

We sample four trajectories per problem from the student before OPD training, using 1,000 DAPO-Math problems. The student and teacher each score the same 5.24M token positions to characterize their disagreement. The interventions then use subsets of these problems, specified below.11 1 Throughout the paper, asterisks indicate statistical significance: ∗p<0.05{}^{*}p<0.05, p∗⁣∗<0.01{}^{**}p<0.01, and ∗∗∗p<0.001{}^{***}p<0.001. Test details and units of analysis are given in App. B.

5.1 Population Statistics

The student and teacher prefer the same next token at most positions, with forks accounting for 13.93% of the rollout. The top 20% of positions ranked by reverse KL contribute 94% of the loss (App. C). At about 63% of profiled forks, the teacher’s preferred token is the student’s second or third choice (App. C). We test whether correcting disagreements improves final answers rather than assuming that loss concentration identifies useful corrections.

5.2 Single Flip

We first ask whether one teacher token can rescue a failed trajectory. We select 10 problems that the teacher solves 4/4 from the prompt and the student 0/4 to make the performance gap observable. We intervene at 5,926 forks across 40 failed trajectories and compare recovery with 16 independent student resamples per prefix. Single-token estimates retain changed-token samples at 5,901 forks; longer segments and continuation counts are specified in Section A.3.

5.2.1 How Much Does a Single Teacher Token Help?

Single-token replacement improves success from 9.91% to 11.31%, a trajectory-weighted gain of 1.41 pp over resampling at the same position (95% CI [0.66,2.15][0.66,2.15], pT<0.001p_{T}<0.001). The problem-weighted gain is 1.22 pp (pP=0.015p_{P}=0.015, Table 1). Extending the teacher’s segment increases the trajectory-weighted mean gain to 3.25 pp at L=16L=16, 16.51 at L=128L=128, and 79.68 when the teacher writes to the end (Section D.1). Whether the inserted token is the teacher’s argmax or a lower-ranked sample makes no detectable difference in the original A100 continuation runs (p=0.27p=0.27). The gain also holds against a keep-token baseline that preserves the original student token and resamples only its continuation (Section D.5).

5.2.2 Which Forks Benefit More from a Single Replacement?

We also report reflection/contrast positions because they may mark a change in reasoning direction, defining them by the teacher’s preferred next token. The average gain varies across fork groups (Table 1). Positions with μtS<0.05\mu_{t}^{S}<0.05 and blind positions show larger gains than their complements, by 1.35 and 3.31 pp respectively under problem-level weighting, with both comparisons significant. The larger gain at blind forks mainly reflects lower student-resampling success rather than much higher replacement success (Section D.3). Reflection/contrast positions have a positive estimated gain over resampling, but neither this gain nor its difference from other forks is significant under the problem-level test. Full group comparisons across intervention lengths are reported in Section D.2.

Despite these differences in average gain, the tested features predict only weakly whether an individual flip outperforms resampling. Combining all features yields a cross-validated AUC of 0.554 (Section D.4). Group averages can favor a selection rule even when the features do not reliably distinguish which flips outperform resampling.

5.2.3 Does Intervention Timing Matter?

Later prefixes are harder to recover even when the teacher completes the continuation (App. E). Paired single-flip gains do not distinguish a position group from the remaining forks under both aggregation levels. Timing primarily describes recoverability rather than incremental token value.

5.2.4 Can the Student Follow a Teacher Correction?

A correction could lead into a continuation the student struggles to follow, but entropy approaches the unchanged-token control after about 40 tokens (Section F.2). On teacher trajectories, 73.4% of fork runs contain only one fork and fewer than 1% reach five tokens (Section F.1), suggesting local rather than sustained disagreement.

5.3 Dual-Track Decoding

We apply repeated flips on 200 randomly sampled problems with four trajectories each. Since flips can shorten or extend trajectories, we compare rules at flip counts of similar magnitude.

5.3.1 How Much Do Repeated Flips Improve Accuracy?

The teacher’s contribution accumulates over repeated corrections rather than requiring the student to follow an entire teacher-generated trajectory (Figure 1). From a student baseline of 28.4%, random flips raise accuracy to 36.1% with about 23 flips per trajectory, 52.0% with 103 flips, and 57.3% with 157 flips. At about 408 flips, covering roughly 90% of forks, accuracy reaches 74.5%, compared with the teacher’s 76.9%. To check whether late teacher hints drive the gains, we stop intervention earlier and let the student finish alone. Gains remain roughly proportional to the preceding flips across exit positions (Section G.2), supporting accumulated correction rather than late answer hints as an explanation for the improvement.

5.3.2 Does Fork Selection Matter?

Both μtT\mu_{t}^{T}- and KL-based selection shift the accuracy curve upward relative to random flips (Figure 1). They achieve higher accuracy with flip counts of similar magnitude. For example, at about 23–26 flips per trajectory, the two rules outperform random selection by 15.4 and 18.1 pp, respectively (both p<10−9p<10^{-9}). The KL curve is slightly higher than the μtT\mu_{t}^{T} curve over much of the tested range. Mass and KL are therefore useful for allocating repeated corrections despite their weak prediction of individual single-flip gains. Ablation experiments across model sizes, model families, and datasets show similar patterns (Sections G.3 to G.5).

5.3.3 Do Reflection Tokens Provide a Particular Advantage?

Reflection-based selection increases the student’s subsequent reflection-word use and trajectory length, but does not significantly improve accuracy over random flips (p=0.29p=0.29, Table 2). In contrast, μtT<10−5\mu_{t}^{T}<10^{-5} achieves significantly higher accuracy than random flips with fewer interventions, without a comparable increase in reflection-word use. Its accuracy advantage over reflection-based selection is not significant (p=0.07p=0.07). More visible reflection is therefore not sufficient evidence of more effective teacher guidance.

5.3.4 Can Teacher Intervention Hurt the Student?

Teacher intervention need not help on every problem, even when the teacher performs better overall. On problems the student solves but the teacher does not, intervention reduces student accuracy from 31.2% to 18.8% in a small subgroup of 16 trajectories (Section G.6). This shows that teacher corrections can also move the student away from a correct answer. Sampled and argmax teacher replacements are compared in Section G.7.

5.4 After OPD

Having examined where the teacher’s advantage lies, we next ask how much of it the student acquires through vanilla OPD. The main analysis uses Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 as teacher and Qwen3-1.7B as student on DAPO-Math. We extend checkpoint analysis to the 4B-to-0.6B and 8B-to-4B Qwen pairs, Llama 3.2 3B-to-1B, and Gemma 3 12B-to-4B. We also examine an instruction-following run of the 1.7B Qwen student evaluated on IFEval (Section A.6.5).

5.4.1 How Does Fork Resolution Change During Training?

We track fork changes by scoring the same pre-training student trajectories with each checkpoint.

  • •

    Solved. An original fork now agrees with the teacher.

  • •

    Unchanged. An original fork retains the pre-training student’s preference.

  • •

    Moved. An original fork chooses neither the teacher’s nor the pre-training student’s token.

  • •

    New. A position where the pre-training student and teacher agreed now disagrees with the teacher.

Fork-group proportions generally change smoothly during training, with few large reversals across model pairs. Solved forks increase and Unchanged forks decrease. In the main Qwen pair, Solved and New proportions settle near 35.5% and 12.9% of the original fork count by Final (Figures 2 and 16). The plateau may reflect limited capacity to acquire further teacher preferences.

However, accuracy does not consistently improve as more forks are resolved and can fluctuate while token agreement improves steadily. This suggests that OPD’s effect on final answers depends on changes beyond agreement with the teacher at fork positions (Section H.1.2).

5.4.2 Which Forks Are More Learnable?

Fork resolution exhibits distinct mass- and KL-based patterns across model pairs rather than a universal ordering (Figures 3 and H.1.4). Runs using the same Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 teacher show similar patterns despite changes in student size or dataset (Section H.1.4). These patterns suggest that the teacher shapes which token choices are easier to learn, while the amount acquired varies with the student and training setting.

Blind forks are less often resolved despite their larger average single-flip gains. In the main Qwen pair, their resolution rate is 14.6%, compared with 37.0% for non-blind forks, consistent with the top-16 loss lacking an explicit supervision term for the teacher’s preferred token.

5.4.3 How Much Does Teacher Intervention Help after OPD?

Mass-based selection remains more effective than random flips at low intervention counts after OPD (Figure 4). Its curves rise steeply and then flatten, while random flips require more interventions to reach similar accuracy. Applying the same mass threshold brings checkpoints with different starting accuracies to similar performance, suggesting that training has not exhausted the useful teacher corrections identified by this rule.

5.4.4 Which Remaining Forks Are Useful Intervention Targets?

We ask whether intervention is more useful at disagreements that persist through training or those introduced by training. At each fork encountered during generation, we also check the pre-training student’s preferred token. If it agrees with the teacher, the fork is New. Otherwise, the fork is Unchanged if the trained student retains its original preference, or Moved if it chooses a different token. We compare these group-based interventions with random flips at counts of similar magnitude.

Prioritizing New or Moved forks does not produce a consistent accuracy advantage across model pairs (Section H.3). In the main Qwen pair, New selection underperforms random controls, while Moved offers no detectable advantage. In Gemma and Llama, neither group significantly improves accuracy over unassisted decoding. Unchanged forks still provide useful corrections, but do not outperform random flips in the Qwen comparisons (Table 3). Newly introduced or changed preferences are therefore weak signals of where further teacher correction will help.

5.4.5 Why Might Fork Resolution Fail to Improve Accuracy?

As shown earlier, repeated flips rescue trajectories and generally recover more accuracy as more corrections are applied. Yet OPD can resolve more forks without improving accuracy, and some runs deteriorate. Fork resolution tracks changes in the preferred token, while generation depends on the full distribution. Entropy remains stable in the main Qwen pair, while late gains in the 8B-to-4B pair accompany declining entropy (Figure 5).

Even where argmax agreement is preserved, entropy rises and the shared token’s probability falls in Llama, Gemma, and IFEval (Table 21). The student therefore becomes less likely to sample that token despite retaining it as its preferred choice. We suspect that training acquires useful corrections while destabilizing choices elsewhere. A good OPD training schedule should help the student resolve more valuable forks while maintaining entropy stability (Section H.4).

6 Conclusion

We systematically study OPD from the KD perspective by separating the value of teacher corrections from the student’s ability to learn them. Evaluating OPD requires measuring both the teacher preferences acquired during training and the accuracy still recoverable through controlled corrections.

Repeated flips recover much more accuracy than a single intervention, and gains continue to accumulate as more corrections are applied. Mass- and KL-based selection allocate repeated corrections more effectively than random flips at counts of similar magnitude, despite weak prediction of individual single-flip gains.

Across model pairs, fork resolution follows smoother trends than accuracy and often approaches a plateau. In the main pair, only 35.5% of original forks are resolved by the final checkpoint. Learnability patterns differ across teachers, and blind forks in the main pair are less often resolved despite their larger intervention gains. Intervention value therefore cannot substitute for evidence of learnability. Selective intervention remains useful after OPD, showing that saturated training accuracy need not mean that the teacher’s useful guidance has been exhausted.

Greater token agreement nevertheless does not consistently produce better answers. Accuracy declines commonly accompany rising entropy across adjacent checkpoints. In several runs, entropy also rises where argmax agreement is preserved and the shared preferred token’s probability falls. These changes motivate our hypothesis that OPD acquires useful corrections while destabilizing choices elsewhere. One direction is selective OPD that downweights New and Moved forks and places more supervision on Unchanged forks. A curriculum could further organize these corrections by their value and learnability, adjusting the pace of supervision to acquire more useful teacher preferences while maintaining distributional stability.

Limitations

Our experiments cover several teacher–student pairs from the Qwen, Llama, and Gemma families, but the tasks are limited to mathematics and instruction following. Token-level interventions require a shared tokenizer within each pair. The single-flip study deliberately selects problems that the teacher solves and the student fails, making teacher corrections easier to observe. Its average gains therefore characterize this selected setting rather than randomly sampled problems.

We separate OPD into two questions: which teacher corrections improve student trajectories, and how the student learns those corrections. Controlled interventions measure the value of corrections, while checkpoint analysis characterizes which teacher preferences are acquired on fixed pre-training prefixes. Determining what makes valuable corrections learnable remains a question for further work. Our proposed training directions still require evaluation of whether they improve learning while preserving distributional stability.

Appendix A Experimental Settings

A.1 Implementation

Intervention and scoring runs use NVIDIA A100 and L40S GPUs on a Slurm cluster, with one process per GPU and both models in bfloat16. Sampling uses vLLM 0.11.0. Dual-track decoding, teacher forcing, and scoring use HuggingFace transformers 4.56.1 and PyTorch 2.8.0 with SDPA attention. Score log-softmax operations use float32. Figures and tables are generated from saved arrays or audited summaries.

All vLLM engines and samplers use seed 0. Dual-track decoding uses a PyTorch generator seeded from the seed, batch index, and shard. Random-flip controls use a NumPy generator with seed 0.

A.2 Population Statistics

For Section 5.1, we use 1,000 problems with 4 student rollouts each, temperature 1.01.0, top-pp 1.01.0, and at most 3,072 new tokens, following the rollout settings of Li et al. (2026). The two next-token distributions at every position are scored with a top-16 truncation.

A.3 Single Flip

Each fork receives four sampled teacher segments of length L∈{1,16,128,∞}L\in\{1,16,128,\infty\} and four student continuations per finite segment. Success is the fraction of continuations ending correct. The 16 independent student resamples per fork yield 94,816 baseline continuations. At L=1L=1, we retain only teacher paths changing the original student token. All four teacher samples repeat that token at 25 positions, leaving 5,901 eligible forks.

At each of the 5,926 forks in Section 5.2, the teacher samples 4 continuations, temperature 0.70.7, top-pp 0.950.95, at most 8,192 tokens in an 8,192-token context. The L∈{1,16,128}L\in\{1,16,128\} segments are prefixes of these, and the student writes 4 continuations of at most 3,072 tokens after each. For the reported L=1L=1 results, we rerun student continuations on NVIDIA L40S GPUs, reusing the same four teacher replacement tokens per fork and drawing four continuations per token. The resample arm also runs on L40S, drawing 16 student continuations directly from each fork prefix. Both arms use the same vLLM pipeline, temperature 0.70.7, top-pp 0.950.95, a 3,072-token generation cap, and a 12,288-token context limit, and are paired by position. Longer-segment outcomes and token-level diagnostics retain the original A100 runs.

A.4 Dual-Track Decoding

For Section 5.3, both models decode in lockstep in transformers, temperature 0.70.7, top-pp 0.950.95, at most 8,192 tokens, with the answer-zone freeze of Section 4.3. The student-alone and teacher-alone rows of Table 12 are 4 vLLM samples per problem with the same settings and the same cap. The teacher pass@4 behind Table 14 uses the 8,192-token cap; an earlier 4,096-token run truncated 38% of the teacher’s answers and was discarded.

Synchronous decoding uses KV caches and batch size 6. Before each replacement decision, we check the last 12 generated tokens for the answer-zone freeze. Each trajectory records token authorship, the student’s sampled token, both argmaxes, and AA and BB.

The additional model-pair and dataset experiments use chunked vLLM decoding. The student generates a chunk of tokens, which the teacher scores under the same prefixes. We accept tokens before the first selected fork, replace its token, discard the remaining chunk, and resume from the corrected prefix. Chunk size controls how many student tokens are generated and scored per round, not the length of teacher intervention. These experiments use chunks of 32 tokens, except for the 4B-to-0.6B KL runs, which use 8.

A.4.1 Reflection-Word List

We use Relay-OPD’s published list of wait, but, hmm, actually, hold, however, yet, oh, alternatively, no, ah, oops, well. Matching ignores case, leading whitespace, and attached punctuation, yielding 79 Qwen3 token ids. Split forms such as Wait followed by punctuation still match the word token. We retain the full list, including words that also have non-reflective uses in mathematics, such as “no solution” and “well-defined”.

A.4.2 Additional Model Pairs

We also use Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 to Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-8B to Qwen3-4B-Base on the same 200 problems, with four trajectories per problem, temperature 0.7, top-pp 0.95, an 8,192-token generation cap, and a 12,288-token context limit. Teacher replacements use argmax and stop at the answer-zone boundary. Reverse KL uses the student’s top-16 tokens plus a residual-probability bucket. Each pair has five mass thresholds, five KL thresholds, and seven random probabilities, all with 800 completed trajectories.

A.4.3 IFEval

We use Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 as teacher and Qwen3-1.7B as student on all 541 official IFEval prompts, with four trajectories per prompt. Standalone baselines and interventions use temperature 0.7, top-pp 0.95, a 6,144-token generation cap, and an 8,192-token context limit, with thinking disabled. We report official strict prompt accuracy, requiring all instructions in a prompt to be satisfied. Interventions use teacher argmax replacements and no answer-zone freeze. Each of the five mass thresholds, five KL thresholds, and seven random probabilities has 2,164 completed trajectories. Fork coverage divides total flips by total argmax disagreements on each policy’s generated trajectories.

A.4.4 Llama Model Pair

We use Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct as teacher and Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct as student on the same 200 DAPO-Math problems. Each of five mass thresholds, five KL thresholds, and seven random probabilities has 800 completed trajectories. Sampling uses temperature 0.7 and top-pp 0.95, with an 8,192-token generation cap and a 12,288-token context limit. Interventions use teacher argmax replacements and the answer-zone freeze. Reverse KL uses the student’s top-16 tokens plus a residual-probability bucket.

A.4.5 Gemma Model Pair

We also evaluate Gemma-3-12B-it as teacher and Gemma-3-4B-it as student on the same 200 DAPO-Math problems, with four trajectories per problem. Sampling uses temperature 0.7 and top-pp 0.95, with an 8,192-token generation cap and a 12,288-token context limit. We compare mass-based, KL-based, and random fork selection using teacher argmax replacements and the answer-zone freeze. Reverse KL uses the student’s top-16 tokens plus a residual-probability bucket.

A.5 Handoff

For each of the 800 dual-track trajectories, we retain the prefix up to a fraction f∈{0.25,0.5,0.75,0.9}f\in\{0.25,0.5,0.75,0.9\} of its length before the answer zone and sample two student continuations. We also include f=1f=1, where the student writes only the answer line, and the student-alone baseline at f=0f=0.

For Section G.2, the student continues each cut trajectory in vLLM, with 2 continuations per cut, temperature 0.70.7, top-pp 0.950.95, and at most 8,192 new tokens within a 12,288-token context.

A.6 After OPD

We train Qwen3-1.7B with vanilla OPD using Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 as teacher. The DAPO-Math training data exclude the 1,000 evaluation problems. The current analysis uses checkpoints at steps 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 48, 64, 128, 192, and the final step 256.

A.6.1 Fork Resolution and Accuracy

Each checkpoint scores all 5,237,483 positions from the same 4,000 pre-training student trajectories. Position identifiers align checkpoint scores with the saved pre-training student and teacher preferences. All 729,574 original argmax forks are included, even if the sampled student token equals the teacher’s argmax. Solved, Unchanged, and Moved partition this set using the definitions in Section 5.4. New forks lie outside the original set.

Accuracy uses each checkpoint’s own 4,000 rollouts on the evaluation problems, with four samples per problem, temperature 1.0, top-pp 1.0, and an 8,192-token generation cap. The pre-training accuracy uses the same settings. Unlike accuracy, fork changes are measured on fixed pre-training prefixes.

A.6.2 Fork Resolution by Pre-Training Scores

We group the original forks using their saved pre-training scores. Teacher mass μtT\mu_{t}^{T} is the teacher’s probability of the base student’s argmax, and reverse KL uses the full vocabulary on the same prefix. Group membership is fixed across checkpoints. Resolution rates divide the number resolved at each checkpoint by the original count within that group. These are pooled position-level rates, not problem-weighted estimates.

A.6.3 Teacher Intervention after OPD

We repeat dual-track decoding at steps 16, 64, and the final checkpoint on the same 200-problem subset, using four trajectories per problem at temperature 0.7 and top-pp 0.95, with an 8,192-token cap. The mass thresholds are 10−410^{-4}, 10−310^{-3}, 10−210^{-2}, and 0.10.1. Random-flip probabilities are 0.060.06, 0.110.11, 0.460.46, and 0.900.90, supplemented by the approximately 100-flip random controls described below. Standalone checkpoint baselines use the same sampling settings. Figure 4 includes only complete 800-trajectory runs.

The additional Final-checkpoint KL interventions in Section H.2 use the student’s top-16 tokens plus a residual-probability bucket. The 0.6B student uses the same 200 mathematics problems and decoding limits. IFEval uses all 541 official prompts, with a 6,144-token generation cap and an 8,192-token context limit. Both settings use temperature 0.7 and top-pp 0.95, with four trajectories per problem or prompt.

A.6.4 Online Fork-Group Selection

The pre-training student, trained student, and teacher score each current prefix to determine its fork group online. This differs from the fixed-prefix composition analysis. These interventions use the same checkpoints and sampling settings as Section A.6.3.

Old, Unchanged, and Random policies use probabilities calibrated toward 100 flips per trajectory. New and Moved policies intervene at every eligible fork, yielding fewer flips. At step 16, New is compared with random probability 0.06 and Moved with 0.11. At steps 64 and 256, both are compared with the approximately 100-flip random control. Step-64 New and Moved runs combine the initial shard with three further shards using the same probability of one, for 800 distinct problem–sample pairs per policy. All realized counts are reported in Table 17.

A.6.5 Additional Checkpoint Evaluations

We evaluate the additional Qwen, Llama, and Gemma checkpoints on 1,000 DAPO-Math problems with four rollouts per problem. The IFEval checkpoints use the 541 official prompts with four rollouts per prompt. These evaluations use temperature 0.7 and top-pp 0.95, with response caps of 8,192 tokens on DAPO-Math and 6,144 on IFEval. The supplementary 1.7B checkpoint curve also uses these sampling settings, separately from the temperature-1.0 evaluation in Table 16. Fork changes use each pair’s own fixed pre-training trajectories and original fork count. We do not pool positions across pairs. Mass and reverse-KL groups retain their pre-training membership at every checkpoint. Fixed-prefix fork statistics are complete at all ten checkpoints for every pair.

The additional Gemma and Llama fork-group interventions use 200 DAPO-Math problems with one rollout per problem at steps 16, 64, and 256. Each policy intervenes at every eligible fork in its selected group, at temperature 0.7 and top-pp 0.95. The response cap is 8,192 tokens and the context cap is 12,288. Intervention stops at the configured answer marker. Resolved positions already share the teacher’s argmax and are not eligible for an argmax flip. These runs report the realized counts without budget calibration. Student-alone controls average four rollouts per problem on the same 200 problems at the same temperature and top-pp. Llama uses the corresponding no-intervention runs from the same decoder. Gemma uses the 200-problem subset of its checkpoint rollouts, with a 9,216-token context cap. We verify that every selected prompt permits the full 8,192-token response cap.

The IFEval fork-group interventions use the same 541 prompts and four trajectories per prompt at steps 16, 64, and 256. Their no-intervention controls use the same sampling settings. Group policies are calibrated using recorded teacher insertions. We verify that each recorded insertion changes the student’s preferred token in these completed runs, so the reported counts are actual flips.

For the entropy analysis in Section H.4, we score each pair’s fixed pre-training trajectories with the base student and every trained checkpoint. We compute full-vocabulary entropy from untempered model probabilities and average over token positions. DAPO-Math includes 4,000 trajectories per pair and IFEval includes 2,164. Scoring stops at the first complete answer when an answer boundary is found, excluding subsequent repetition. Accuracy uses each checkpoint’s own rollouts at temperature 0.7 and top-pp 0.95.

Appendix B Statistical Tests

The tests distinguish whether teacher intervention helps from whether one group or selection rule helps more than its comparator. Positions within a trajectory and trajectories from the same problem can be correlated, so we aggregate differences before testing rather than treating every fork as an independent observation. All reported tt-tests are two-sided. Group-comparison pp-values are unadjusted for multiple testing and interpreted as exploratory. Asterisks refer to the comparison specified in each table.

B.1 Single-Flip Tests

We ask whether a teacher replacement improves recovery beyond another student attempt from the same prefix. At each fork, we subtract the success rate of 16 independent student resamples from the teacher-intervention success rate. Comparing continuations from the same prefix controls for how recoverable that position already is without the teacher. At L=1L=1, only teacher paths changing the original token contribute, leaving 5,901 of 5,926 positions eligible. All teacher paths contribute at longer lengths.

Trajectory-Level Gain (pTp_{T}).

To estimate the average gain across failed trajectories, we average paired position gains within each trajectory and apply a one-sample tt-test against zero to the 40 trajectory means (pTp_{T}). Each trajectory receives equal weight. Reported single-flip confidence intervals use the Student-tt distribution.

Problem-Level Gain (pPp_{P}).

To assess the gain across problems while aggregating their correlated trajectories, we pool eligible position gains within each problem and test the 10 problem means against zero (pPp_{P}). Each problem receives equal weight, so this test changes both the unit of analysis and the weighting relative to pTp_{T}.

Bootstrap Check.

We use 2,000 trajectory-bootstrap replicates to check the sensitivity of the overall gain interval to the Student-tt construction. Each replicate resamples whole trajectory means rather than individual forks.

Fork-Group Differences.

A positive gain over resampling does not establish that a group is more useful than other forks. We therefore compare the group’s mean paired gain with the mean paired gain at the remaining positions. Within each trajectory or problem, we subtract the latter from the former and test these contrasts against zero. Each included unit must contain at least three eligible positions on each side. A positive significant contrast indicates a larger average teacher-intervention gain in that group, rather than merely a higher absolute recovery rate. Full estimates and tests, including nonsignificant comparisons, appear in Sections D.2 and D.3. Predicting the benefit of an individual flip is a separate question, addressed in Section D.4.

B.2 Dual-Track Tests

Each policy generates four trajectories on the same 200 randomly sampled problems. For each problem, we subtract the comparator’s mean correctness from the tested policy’s mean correctness, then apply a one-sample tt-test against zero to the 200 differences. This is equivalent to a paired tt-test on the two sets of problem means. Pairing is over problems, not individual trajectories, because the policies generate different continuations.

Fork Selection versus Random Flips.

This comparison asks whether choosing forks by a feature improves accuracy over random intervention. We apply the problem-paired test above to the selected policy and its random control. Controls approximate intervention coverage or counts, as specified for each experiment, rather than matching the exact realized number of flips. Random-control settings and comparison results for the original model pair are reported in Section G.1.

Teacher Sampling versus Argmax.

This comparison asks whether sampling a teacher token changes accuracy relative to taking the teacher’s argmax under the same selection rule. We apply the same problem-paired test to the two complete policies (Table 15).

Fork-Group Selection after OPD.

This comparison asks whether a fork’s training history identifies useful intervention targets. We compare each group-selection policy with its designated random control using the same problem-paired test. Control choices and realized counts are specified in Sections A.6.4 and H.3.

Wilcoxon Check.

For the original random-control comparisons, we also apply a Wilcoxon signed-rank test to the problem-level differences. This checks sensitivity to the paired tt-test’s treatment of those differences and gives the same significance conclusions.

Welch Check.

For the same comparisons, a Welch tt-test compares the 800 trajectory outcomes from each policy without pairing individual trajectories. This alternative aggregation also gives the same significance conclusions, while the problem-paired test remains the reported comparison.

B.3 Handoff Tests

Constant-Gain Residuals.

This test asks whether accuracy at each teacher exit point departs from a constant-gain-per-flip model. Predicted accuracy at exit fraction ff interpolates between the problem’s student-alone rate and the trajectory’s accuracy at f=1f=1, weighted by the fraction of flips made before ff. We subtract this prediction from observed recovery and test the mean residual against zero over the 800 trajectories, then repeat the test after averaging within each problem.

Exit-Position Trend.

This test asks whether departures from the constant-gain model vary systematically with the teacher’s exit position. We fit a residual slope against ff within each trajectory and test the mean slope against zero. Results for both handoff tests appear in Section G.2.

Appendix C Population Statistics

The profiles use forks where the sampled student token also differs from the teacher’s argmax, covering 12.23% of all positions. A sampled-token mismatch alone need not be a fork, since sampling can select a different token even when both argmaxes agree. Loss concentration in Figure 6 uses all positions without this filtering. Most probability mass lies on the top two or three candidates of either model. The teacher’s argmax is the student’s second choice at 46% of profiled forks and its third at 17%. In either ranking direction, the other model’s argmax falls outside the top-16 at 7–8% of these forks. These profiles distinguish disagreements over highly ranked alternatives from blind forks where the teacher’s preferred token is outside the student’s top-16.

Appendix D Single-Flip Gains

D.1 Overall Gains by Intervention Length

For L=1L=1, the trajectory-weighted gain is 0.014070.01407 (95% CI [0.00662,0.02153][0.00662,0.02153], p=0.00047p=0.00047), and the problem-weighted gain is 0.012200.01220 (p=0.0152p=0.0152). As a weighting sensitivity check, averaging trajectory means equally within each problem gives 0.014070.01407 (p=0.0207p=0.0207).

Teacher Argmax versus Lower-Ranked Replacements.

The original A100 runs show no detectable difference between teacher-argmax and lower-ranked replacements (p=0.27p=0.27).

D.2 Gains by Fork Group

The group comparisons distinguish whether teacher intervention helps from whether a group benefits more than other forks. A positive gain over resampling answers the first question, while the group-versus-rest contrast answers the second (Table 7). Some contrasts pass the trajectory-level test but not the problem-level test, so their significance depends on the aggregation and weighting. For longer segments, the outcome includes additional teacher tokens and cannot be attributed to the first replacement alone (Tables 5 and 6).

D.3 Group Eligibility and Success Rates

Larger intervention gains do not necessarily identify positions with the highest recovery rates. Blind forks have larger gains than non-blind forks, but their replacement success rates are much closer than their resampling success rates (Table 8). Their larger gain mainly reflects the lower resampling success at these positions. The two tables also use different eligibility rules. Table 7 estimates within-group gains using all units with eligible positions, while Table 8 retains trajectories with at least three eligible positions in both the group and its complement. This changes the positions and trajectory weights contributing to the estimates, including the reported reflection gain.

D.4 Predicting Single-Flip Gains over Resampling

For prediction at L=1L=1, the label is whether estimated true-flip success exceeds the independently estimated resample rate at the same fork. Of 5,901 eligible positions, 3,303 are tied and excluded, leaving 2,598 labels with 1,333 positives. These labels concern individual forks rather than group-mean gains.

Logistic regression uses five-fold cross-validation grouped by trajectory, with numeric and one-hot token-class features standardized within each training fold. The 95% intervals use 100 trajectory-bootstrap refits, keeping duplicate copies of a trajectory in the same fold. We report AUC only at L=1L=1 because longer teacher continuations do not isolate the initial token’s predictive value.

D.5 Keep-Token Baseline

The keep arm preserves the original student token at each of the 5,926 fork prefixes and independently samples 16 continuations, giving 94,816 outcomes. It uses the same L40S continuation pipeline and decoding settings as the replacement and resample arms. True-flip comparisons retain the same 5,901 eligible positions as the main analysis. Resample versus keep uses all 5,926 positions.

Replacement improves over keep under both aggregation-level tests. Resample and keep do not differ detectably (Table 10).

Appendix E Intervention Timing and Recovery

The success rates below average positions, whereas paired gains average within trajectories before averaging across trajectories. Subtracting the displayed success rates therefore need not reproduce the trajectory-weighted gains.

Absolute recovery declines at later positions under both teacher intervention and student resampling (Table 11). After accounting for resampling, no single-token position group differs from the remaining forks under both trajectory- and problem-level tests. Position therefore does not reliably distinguish which single-token interventions provide larger gains. Across all tested intervention lengths, however, gains fall from the penultimate to the final decile (Figure 9). This drop is largest when the teacher completes the continuation, from 81.4 to 56.1 pp. Longer interventions measure the continuation’s contribution rather than that of the initial token.

Appendix F Student Ability to Follow Teacher Corrections

F.1 Fork Spacing on Teacher Trajectories

We score 4,000 teacher-generated trajectories with the student and teacher, identifying forks at 2.11M of 15.17M positions. Fork spacing is the position difference between successive forks within the same trajectory. A consecutive run is a maximal sequence of adjacent forks.

The median distance between successive forks is three tokens, and 27.9% occur at adjacent positions (Figure 10). Although 47.0% of forks belong to runs of at least two tokens, most runs contain only one or two tokens. These short runs suggest that disagreement on teacher trajectories is usually local rather than sustained over long stretches.

F.2 Student Responses after a Teacher Correction

We examine difficulty following teacher corrections through student entropy and teacher-token probability. The unchanged-token control retains teacher samples reproducing the original student token at 1,495 positions, with 1,470 admitting both changed and unchanged paths. This control is used only for these diagnostics, not as the independent resample baseline.

Student entropy is elevated for about 40 tokens after a replacement before approaching the unchanged-token control (Figure 11a). On the teacher’s continuation, student entropy tracks teacher entropy within 0.050.05 nats (b). The probability the student assigns to teacher tokens rises from 0.610.61 to 0.830.83, remaining 0.060.06 to 0.130.13 below the teacher’s own probability (c).

Appendix G Additional Dual-Track Results

G.1 Complete Results for the Main Model Pair

Random controls use preset selection probabilities chosen to approximate trigger coverage. We report realized flip counts because each policy changes its subsequent trajectory, so coverage matching does not imply equal flip counts.

The original controls give accuracy differences of +0.138+0.138 ([0.099,0.176][0.099,0.176], p<10−10p<10^{-10}) for μtT<0.1\mu_{t}^{T}<0.1 versus random 46%, and +0.133+0.133 ([0.093,0.173][0.093,0.173], p<10−9p<10^{-9}) for μtT<0.05\mu_{t}^{T}<0.05 versus random 35%. Reflection-word selection versus random 6% gives +0.020+0.020 ([−0.017,0.057][-0.017,0.057], p=0.29p=0.29). The sparse μtT<10−5\mu_{t}^{T}<10^{-5} rule gives +0.055+0.055 ([0.018,0.092][0.018,0.092], p=0.004p=0.004) versus random 6% and +0.035+0.035 ([−0.003,0.073][-0.003,0.073], p=0.07p=0.07) versus reflection-word selection.

Additional random controls use probabilities 0.11 and 0.22. Against 0.11, μtT<10−3\mu_{t}^{T}<10^{-3} gains 15.375 pp (p=1.18×10−10p=1.18\times 10^{-10}), and KL>5\mathrm{KL}>5 gains 18.125 pp (p=8.02×10−14p=8.02\times 10^{-14}). Against 0.22, KL>4\mathrm{KL}>4 gains 12.75 pp (p=1.36×10−9p=1.36\times 10^{-9}). All comparisons use the same problem-paired test.

G.2 Handoff

We are concerned that the accuracy gains may come from the teacher supplying the answer near the end of the trajectory. We therefore stop teacher intervention at earlier fractions ff of each dual-track trajectory before the answer zone and let the student complete the reasoning and answer alone with no further flips (Section A.5). Varying ff from 0 (the student alone) to 1 (the full dual-track trajectory) measures accuracy as a function of how far the teacher’s corrections extend.

G.2.1 Gains across Teacher Exit Positions

Accuracy gains accumulate roughly in proportion to the number of flips across teacher exit positions, with an average gain of 0.10–0.11 pp per flip (Figure 12). This suggests that the teacher’s contribution is spread across the trajectory rather than concentrated in a narrow region.

Each dual-track trajectory is cut at ⌊f⋅tans⌉\lfloor f\cdot t_{\mathrm{ans}}\rceil, where tanst_{\mathrm{ans}} is the first position of the answer-zone marker. We grade the complete text after the student finishes using the settings in App. A. At f=1f=1, the student writes only the answer line (median 10 tokens), with accuracy 0.7570.757 compared with dual-track accuracy 0.7450.745.

Under the constant-gain-per-flip model in Section B.3, mean prediction residuals range from −0.02-0.02 to −0.01-0.01. Trajectory-level tests give p=0.06p=0.06, 0.200.20, 0.060.06, and 0.340.34 at f=0.25f=0.25, 0.50.5, 0.750.75, and 0.90.9, respectively. All problem-level tests give p≥0.13p\geq 0.13, and the residual-slope test gives p=0.47p=0.47.

G.3 Ablation across Model Sizes

We test two additional teacher–student pairs within the Qwen family, Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 to Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-8B to Qwen3-4B-Base (Section A.4.2). Both pairs show the same overall pattern as the original 4B-to-1.7B pair (Figure 13). Mass- and KL-based selection achieve higher accuracy than random flips at intervention counts of similar magnitude, while increasing random flips also improves accuracy.

G.4 Ablation on a Different Dataset

We repeat the interventions on official IFEval using the original Qwen teacher–student pair. Mass- and KL-based selection remain beneficial, especially at low flip budgets, while random selection gradually approaches the selective curves as coverage increases (Figure 14).

Yet accuracy remains around 76% even when nearly 90% of forks are flipped, below the teacher’s 83.9%. High fork coverage does not reproduce teacher-only generation because the student still samples its own tokens wherever the models share the same argmax. The teacher may place greater probability on the correct token or assign more probability to suitable alternatives. These possibilities motivate further study of the teacher’s advantage beyond argmax disagreements.

G.5 Ablation across Model Families

We also test Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct as teacher and Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct as student on DAPO-Math (Section A.4.4). Mass-based selection achieves higher accuracy than random flips at similar intervention counts (Figure 15). At approximately 20–25 flips per trajectory, accuracy is 8.4% with mass-based selection, 6.5% with KL-based selection, and 4.4% with random selection.

The same KL threshold covers substantially fewer forks in this pair. KL>1\mathrm{KL}>1 selects 28.8% of encountered Llama forks, compared with 49.5–74.5% in the two additional Qwen pairs using the same estimator (Figures 13 and A.4.2). Thus, a fixed KL threshold does not provide comparable intervention coverage across model pairs, even though mass-based selection remains useful in the Llama setting.

G.6 Results by Problem Group

Teacher intervention can also reduce accuracy on problems the student can solve but the teacher cannot (Table 14). In this group of 16 trajectories, accuracy falls from 31.2% for the student alone to 18.8% under either tested mass threshold. This small subgroup illustrates that replacing student choices with teacher choices is not uniformly beneficial, even when the teacher performs better overall.

Problem groups use the student and teacher’s standalone pass@4 on these same 200 problems. A model counts as solving a problem if at least one of its four samples is correct.

G.7 Teacher Sampling versus Argmax

Teacher sampling improves accuracy at μtT<0.05\mu_{t}^{T}<0.05, while the other two thresholds show no significant difference from argmax replacement. A problem-level Wilcoxon check supports the same conclusion at thresholds 0.1 and 0.05 (p=0.61997p=0.61997 and p=0.01027p=0.01027). These comparisons evaluate complete online policies because sampled replacements can change subsequent prefixes.

Appendix H After OPD

H.1 Accuracy and Fork Resolution across Checkpoints

H.1.1 Original Qwen Pair

Table 16 reports accuracy on each checkpoint’s own rollouts and fork changes on the fixed pre-training prefixes. Experimental settings are given in Section A.6.1.

H.1.2 Additional Model Pairs and IFEval

The relationship between fork resolution and accuracy differs across model pairs (Figure 16). In the 4B-to-0.6B pair, both improve rapidly early in training and then change more slowly. The 8B-to-4B pair has a different trajectory, with most of its accuracy increase occurring later. Thus, the timing of the gains in the original 1.7B student does not describe every OPD run.

Llama, Gemma, and IFEval show that increasing token agreement need not improve answers. By the final checkpoint, 22.1% of original Llama forks, 32.5% of Gemma forks, and 15.1% of IFEval forks are solved. Their accuracy does not follow the same increase. Gemma resolves almost a third of its original forks while its final accuracy remains close to its early-checkpoint accuracy. Fork resolution therefore measures an aspect of learning that accuracy alone does not reveal, but agreement on reference prefixes is not sufficient to ensure better answers on the student’s own rollouts. Evaluation settings are given in Section A.6.5.

H.1.3 Composition of Resolved Forks

Group definitions and aggregation for Figure 3 are given in Section A.6.2.

Figure 17 instead describes the composition of the final resolved set. At step 256, 258,841 original forks are resolved. Forks with μtT<0.05\mu_{t}^{T}<0.05 comprise 39.7% of the original set but 50.7% of the resolved set. The most extreme groups remain small despite their higher resolution rates. Forks with μtT<10−5\mu_{t}^{T}<10^{-5} comprise 2.3% of original forks and 4.0% of resolved forks, while forks with reverse KL below 0.1 comprise 1.0% and 1.4%, respectively.

H.1.4 Fork Resolution by Mass and KL across Pairs

The strong mass ordering in the original 1.7B student also appears in the 0.6B student (Figure 18). Its final resolution rate declines from 56.7% at μtT<10−5\mu_{t}^{T}<10^{-5} to 22.8% at μtT≥0.3\mu_{t}^{T}\geq 0.3. The 8B-to-4B pair does not show the same monotonic ordering. Its lowest-mass group is not the most frequently resolved, and the reverse-KL profile also differs from the smaller students.

Lower-mass groups are more frequently resolved in Llama and IFEval, but the differences are smaller than in the 0.6B student (Figures 19 and 20). IFEval retains this ordering despite the absence of an overall accuracy increase. These profiles show why the usefulness of a selection score for online correction and its relationship to learning must be examined separately.

H.2 KL Interventions at the Final Checkpoint

H.2.1 Additional Qwen Model Size

Teacher correction remains useful after OPD in the 4B-to-0.6B pair (Figure 21). At Final, KL-based intervention with KL>3\mathrm{KL}>3 raises accuracy from 27.88% to 58.75% with about 105 flips per trajectory. Thus, training leaves substantial accuracy recoverable through further teacher correction in this smaller student as well.

H.2.2 Instruction Following

Further teacher correction also improves instruction following after OPD. On IFEval, Final-checkpoint accuracy rises from 66.27% without intervention to 72.04% with KL>3\mathrm{KL}>3 and about 18 flips per trajectory. Increasing coverage with KL>1\mathrm{KL}>1 reaches 74.03% with about 84 flips. These results extend the residual recovery observed in mathematics to instruction following.

H.3 Interventions by Fork Group

H.3.1 Original Qwen Pair

Table 17 reports the complete current-run results. Online group assignment, calibration, and random controls are described in Section A.6.4.

The pp values in Table 17 use two-sided paired tt-tests over the 200 problem means, each averaging four outcomes (Section B.2). These exploratory comparisons are unadjusted.

H.3.2 Gemma and Llama

New and Moved selection provide limited recovery in Gemma across the tested checkpoints (Table 18). At final, their accuracies are 32.5% and 30.5%, compared with 32.0% without intervention. Old and Unchanged selection instead reach 43.0%, using more flips. Under these policies, most of the observed recovery comes from correcting forks that retain the base student’s preference rather than newly introduced or moved forks.

New and Moved selection also remain close to student-alone accuracy in Llama (Table 19). At final, both reach 3.5%, compared with 1.6% without intervention and 6.0% under Unchanged selection. The gains are smaller than in Gemma, and the group ranking varies across checkpoints.

Gemma’s remaining Old forks still admit useful correction at later checkpoints. Selecting Old forks reaches 41.0% accuracy at step 16 and 43.0% at final, with about 79 and 67 flips per trajectory (Table 18). The persistence of this recovery contrasts with the limited accuracy improvement during training. Llama does not show a comparably strong recovery under these group policies (Table 19). The benefit of post-training intervention must therefore be measured for each pair rather than inferred from the fraction of forks resolved.

H.3.3 IFEval

None of the four group policies yields a consistent accuracy improvement across IFEval checkpoints at the tested low flip counts (Table 20). Differences from student-alone accuracy range from −1.06-1.06 to +0.65+0.65 pp, with 0.44 to 0.58 flips per trajectory. New and Moved selection therefore add little recovery in this setting, but the same is true of Old and Unchanged selection at these counts.

H.4 Distribution Changes Beyond Fork Resolution

H.4.1 Why Might More Resolved Forks Fail to Improve Accuracy?

Fork resolution increases in Llama, Gemma, and IFEval without a corresponding increase in accuracy (Figure 16). Resolving an argmax disagreement changes the student’s preferred token, while generation depends on the full token distribution. The usefulness of the acquired preferences and accompanying changes in token probabilities are therefore separate questions when agreement increases without better answers.

Mean entropy on the same pre-training prefixes rises substantially in these three settings (Figure 22). From Base to Final, it rises from 0.169 to 0.345 nats in Llama, from 0.150 to 0.315 in Gemma, and from 0.248 to 0.653 on IFEval. The original 1.7B Qwen student’s entropy remains near 0.250 nats, while the 0.6B student’s changes from 0.334 to 0.285. Both Qwen students improve in accuracy. The 8B-to-4B pair follows a different trajectory, with final entropy above Base but late accuracy gains accompanying a decline from its intermediate entropy peak.

These entropy trajectories motivate examining whether training changes the distribution at positions where the student already agrees with the teacher. Such changes are invisible to fork resolution because the preferred token can remain the same while its probability changes.

H.4.2 Probability Changes at Originally Agreed Positions

We retain the same pre-answer positions where the base student and teacher share an argmax. Original Non-Forks includes all these positions. Still Agree further requires the final checkpoint to retain that shared argmax. Each row compares Base and Final on exactly the same positions. Entropy uses the full vocabulary, and probabilities are untempered. When the teacher’s token falls outside the saved top-16, its probability is bounded by the sixteenth token’s probability rather than set to zero.

Entropy increases even on Still Agree positions, from 0.112 to 0.251 nats in Llama, 0.097 to 0.230 in Gemma, and 0.082 to 0.279 on IFEval. The shared token’s untempered probability falls by 2.20, 3.54, and 4.20 pp in these settings. These changes therefore extend beyond newly introduced forks. The original 1.7B and 0.6B Qwen students instead show lower entropy and higher shared-token probability on these positions. The 8B-to-4B pair improves accuracy despite higher final entropy and lower shared-token probability than Base. Its late accuracy gains accompany a decline from the intermediate entropy peak, making the trajectory of distributional change more informative than the Base-to-Final difference alone.
